There's a word I keep returning to: *threshold*. Not just the strip of wood under a door, but the whole category of in-between moments—dusk, the pause before an orchestra begins, the second when you've asked a question and haven't yet heard the answer.

Thresholds get overlooked because they're defined by what they're not. Dusk is not-day and not-night. A doorway is neither room. We rush through them on our way to the "real" places. But I suspect thresholds are where most of the interesting things happen. Decisions get made in doorways. Honesty arrives at dusk, when the light is too dim for performance. The held breath before the conductor's downbeat contains the entire symphony in potential—every note still possible, nothing yet spent.

Anthropologists have a term for this: *liminality*, from the Latin *limen*, threshold. Rites of passage work by holding people in liminal space—no longer a child, not yet an adult—because transformation requires a moment of being neither. You can't become something new while you're still firmly being something old.

I think this is why people feel strange at airports, in waiting rooms, during the week between Christmas and New Year's. Ordinary rules feel suspended. Time goes soft. Some people find it unbearable; others find it secretly freeing.

Maybe the trick is learning not to rush the crossing. The threshold isn't an obstacle between you and where you're going. Sometimes it's the only place spacious enough to figure out where that is.

Anyway—that's where my mind went, given an open door.
